title: Exam Week
subtitle: Shapes, decimals, fractions, ratio. One paper, and an estimate before every answer.
objectives: Recall the ten Math topics of the term
Estimate first to reject an impossible answer
Show working so a slip does not cost everything
Name the traps that cost the most marks

cards.title: Four topics, ten weeks, one paper
cards.text: Shapes and transformations, decimals, fractions, and ratio. Every one of them is still examinable.

cards.title: Ten weeks, one tap each
cards.text: This is your revision sheet. The second line of each is the mistake that costs the mark.

cards.title: Estimate before you calculate
cards.text: An estimate cannot give you the answer. It can tell you instantly that an answer is impossible.
points: **Round both numbers.** Do it in your head.
**An answer of 250** is now obviously wrong.
**Five seconds** catches a misplaced decimal point.

question.text: You estimate 0.48 × 51 as about 25. Your working gives 244.8. What has happened?
options: The decimal point is in the wrong place
question.explain: Estimating cannot give the answer, but it catches an answer that is out by a factor of ten.

cards.title: Nobody checks a lap time against nothing
cards.text: A driver knows roughly what a lap should take. A reading two seconds out means the timing is wrong, not the car.
points: **You need a rough expectation** to spot an error.
**Without one**, any number looks fine.
**The estimate is the expectation.**
**Make it before you start**, not after.

cards.title: Write the steps down, even when you can see it
cards.text: A wrong answer with visible working can still earn method marks. A wrong answer on its own earns nothing.
points: **One line per step.**
**Keep the decimal points in a column.**
**Do not rub out** a step you replaced.
**Working is evidence**, not decoration.

question.text: Showing your working can earn marks even when the final answer is wrong.
question.explain: Method marks are real. An answer alone is all or nothing.

cards.title: Good place to pause
cards.text: Part 2 is the traps and the exam room. The paper after it is 24 questions.

cards.title: Three errors account for most lost marks
cards.text: They are not hard ideas. They are habits from an earlier topic being used in the wrong one.

cards.title: Right method, wrong topic
cards.text: Each of these is correct somewhere else in the course, which is exactly why it is easy to reach for.
points: **Lining up points** is adding, not multiplying.
**A common denominator** is adding, not multiplying.
**Flipping** is only the second fraction.
**Ask which topic** the question is in.

cards.title: The right move in the wrong situation still loses
cards.text: A block is correct against one attack and useless against another. Knowing the move is not the same as reading the moment.
points: **You know all four methods already.**
**Choosing is the tested skill.**
**Name the topic first**, then start.
**Most errors are a choice error.**

cards.title: A number with no unit is half an answer
cards.text: Pesos, centimetres, kilograms. If the question had units, the answer needs them too.
points: **Copy the unit** from the question.
**Check it makes sense.** Money to two places.
**Metres and centimetres** are a common trap.
**Write it every time.**

question.text: Which method belongs to multiplying fractions?
options: Multiply straight across, no common denominator needed
question.explain: A common denominator is for adding and subtracting. Flipping is for dividing, and only the second fraction.

cards.title: The last ten minutes are for checking
cards.text: Finishing early is not the goal. Going back through with fresh eyes catches the slips your first pass made.
points: **Recheck the estimates first.**
**Then the units.**
**Then anything you marked** to come back to.
**Never hand it in early.**

question.text: Finishing a maths paper early and handing it in is a good use of the time.
question.explain: The spare time is for checking estimates, units and the questions you skipped.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Estimate first.** It catches the decimal point.
**Show the working.** Method marks are real.
**Name the topic** before choosing a method.
**Write the unit** on every answer.

quiz.text: Which three regular polygons tessellate on their own?
quiz.explain: Week 1. Their interior angles divide exactly into 360 degrees.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

quiz.text: What is the interior angle of a regular hexagon?
quiz.explain: Week 1. Three of them meet at a vertex, because 3 times 120 is exactly 360.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

quiz.text: Why does a regular pentagon not tessellate?
options: Its 108 degree angle does not divide into 360
It is not a convex shape
quiz.explain: Week 1. Three pentagons give 324 degrees and leave a gap; four would overlap.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

quiz.text: What is needed to describe a rotation fully?
options: The angle, the centre and the direction
quiz.explain: Week 2. Without a centre and a direction it cannot be reproduced.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

quiz.text: Translation, reflection and rotation all keep the shape the same size.
quiz.explain: Week 2. Size and angles are preserved by all three. Only the position or orientation changes.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

quiz.text: What is 3.7 + 0.45?
quiz.explain: Week 3. Align the decimal points and pad 3.7 to 3.70.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

quiz.text: What is 5 − 2.35?
quiz.explain: Week 3. Write 5 as 5.00 first, then subtract in columns.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

quiz.text: Which is larger, 0.45 or 0.5?
quiz.explain: Week 4. Pad to 0.45 and 0.50, then compare from the left. More digits does not mean bigger.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

quiz.text: 3.5 and 3.50 are the same number.
quiz.explain: Week 4. A trailing zero changes nothing. It only helps the columns line up.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

quiz.text: What is 0.4 × 0.3?
quiz.explain: Week 5. Multiply 4 by 3, then count two decimal places across both factors.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

quiz.text: What is 6 ÷ 0.5?
quiz.explain: Week 5. How many halves fit into six? Dividing by less than one makes a number bigger.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

quiz.text: What is 2.6 × 100?
quiz.explain: Week 5. The digits move two places to the left when multiplying by 100.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

quiz.text: What is 2 + 3 × 4?
quiz.explain: Week 6. Multiplication comes before addition, so it is 2 + 12.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

quiz.text: Which is better value: 250 g for ₱75, or 400 g for ₱116?
options: They cost the same per gram
quiz.explain: Week 6. ₱0.30 per gram against ₱0.29 per gram. Only the unit rate can tell you.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

quiz.text: What is 4.687 rounded to two decimal places?
quiz.explain: Week 6. Only the digit immediately to the right of the place matters, and 7 rounds up.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

quiz.text: What is 1/2 + 1/3?
quiz.explain: Week 7. Common denominator 6 gives 3/6 + 2/6. Never add the bottoms.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

quiz.text: What is 3/4 − 1/6?
quiz.explain: Week 7. Common denominator 12 gives 9/12 − 2/12.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

quiz.text: What is 8/12 in its lowest terms?
quiz.explain: Week 7. Both divide by 4. Keep going until nothing divides both.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

quiz.text: What is 2/3 × 3/4?
quiz.explain: Week 8. Multiply straight across for 6/12, which simplifies to 1/2. No common denominator needed.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

quiz.text: What is 1/2 ÷ 1/4?
quiz.explain: Week 8. Flip the second fraction only: 1/2 × 4/1. Dividing by a fraction makes it bigger.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

quiz.text: In a ratio of 3 : 4, how many parts are there in total?
quiz.explain: Week 9. Three parts and four parts. Seven is the total, not one of the numbers.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

quiz.text: Share ₱350 in the ratio 3 : 4. What are the two amounts?
quiz.explain: Week 9. Seven parts, so one part is ₱50. Then 3 × 50 and 4 × 50.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

quiz.text: On a 1 : 100 scale drawing, a wall measures 4 cm. How long is the real wall?
quiz.explain: Week 10. 4 × 100 is 400 cm, which is 4 m. The real thing is bigger than the drawing.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

quiz.text: If one worker builds a wall in 6 days, two workers always build it in 3.
quiz.explain: Week 10. Not everything scales in proportion, and the exam relies on that assumption being made.
quiz.objective: Recall the ten Math topics of the term

teacher.summary: Week 11 is exam week for Math and teaches no new content. The deck is built around the three things that actually move a Grade 6 maths mark: estimating before calculating, writing working down so method marks survive a slip, and naming the topic before choosing a method. That last one matters most here, because almost every error in this term's material is a correct method borrowed from the wrong topic — lining up decimal points when multiplying, finding a common denominator when multiplying fractions, flipping both fractions when dividing. Every number in the 24-question paper has been checked programmatically.
discussion: Ask him to estimate before every answer for the whole paper, out loud. It is the single highest-value habit here.
Ask which topic a question belongs to before he starts it.
Ask what a common denominator is actually for, and where it is not needed.
After the paper, sort the misses into 'did not know' and 'knew but slipped'. They need different fixes.
teacher.extension: Give him five answers that are wrong only by a factor of ten and ask him to catch them by estimating alone. It builds the habit faster than doing the questions properly.
misconceptions: 'Working is only for hard questions.' Method marks are real, and an answer alone is all or nothing.
'Line up the decimal points' applied to multiplication. That rule belongs to addition and subtraction.
'Multiplying fractions needs a common denominator.' It does not. That is only for adding and subtracting.
'Finishing early is good.' The spare minutes are for checking estimates, units and skipped questions.
